opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this came up when we were writing and reviewing questions for GPQA. "Boiling temperature" sounds like a perfectly well-defined physical quantity, but it isn't really, unless you specify the conditions. Boiling point depends heavily on pressure. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at one standard atmosphere, but at altitude it boils noticeably lower, and in a pressure cooker it's higher. So if a question just asks "what's the boiling temperature of this compound," an expert reading it carefully might reasonably ask: at what pressure? Are we talking about the normal boiling point, at one atmosphere, or the standard boiling point, which IUPAC defines at one bar? Those differ slightly, and for some questions that difference can matter.

And there's more. For mixtures you don't have a single boiling temperature at all. You have a range, or you have to think about azeotropes. For some substances the measured value depends on purity, or the compound decomposes before it boils, so the "boiling point" in a reference table is extrapolated or measured under reduced pressure.

The broader point, and why we cared about it, is that when you're trying to write questions that are genuinely hard but still have objectively correct answers, ambiguity like this is poison. If a question is underspecified, then when an expert validator gets it "wrong," you can't tell whether they lacked the knowledge or just resolved the ambiguity differently than the question writer intended. So a lot of the expert feedback process was people flagging exactly these things: "this term is fine for a textbook, but for a precise question you need to pin it down." Boiling temperature was a nice illustrative case of a phrase that feels totally unambiguous to a non-expert and turns out to hide several assumptions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the phrase sounds totally unambiguous when you first hear it, but once you actually try to pin it down you realize it's underspecified in a way that matters a lot for evaluation. Boiling temperature of what? Under what pressure? Most people have in mind "water at one atmosphere, a hundred degrees Celsius," but that's a whole bundle of assumptions that nobody stated. If you're writing a question that's supposed to have a single, gradable, objectively correct answer, you have to make those assumptions explicit, because otherwise you can get an answer that is perfectly correct given a reasonable reading of the question but gets marked wrong by the grader.

And this was a recurring theme for us when we were building GPQA. A huge fraction of the work wasn't coming up with hard questions, it was making sure the hard questions were actually well-posed. Experts in a field are so used to the implicit conventions that they don't notice they're relying on them. So a chemist writes "boiling temperature" and in their head it obviously means at standard pressure, but a careful reader, or a careful model, might say "well, it depends," and that's a legitimate response. We wanted the disagreements between the question writer and the expert validators to reflect genuine difficulty, not just ambiguity in how the question was phrased. So we spent a lot of effort on that feedback loop, where validators would flag things like this and the writer would revise.

I think it's also a nice small example of a bigger point about evaluating models. When a model gets something "wrong," you really want to know whether it was wrong about the world or whether it just interpreted the question differently than you did. Those have very different implications, and sloppy question wording collapses them together.

Even for water, the familiar answer of 100 degrees Celsius assumes a particular pressure.
